A: For seventy years, Harbor Rowing Club has selected crews through timed trials on the same stretch of river. Coach Mila wants to use indoor power data and video analysis instead, giving athletes more precise feedback, but alumni see the river trial as the ceremony that binds each generation. Should Mila adopt data-based selection or preserve the traditional river trials?
B: Residents have always begun their spring cleanup by gathering at dawn and drawing street assignments from an old wooden box. Coordinator Theo could replace the ritual with an app that assigns routes efficiently and tracks missed areas, but neighbors treasure the shared opening. Should Theo introduce the app or keep the familiar draw that marks the season?
C: Cricket umpire Sanjay promised to officiate a youth semifinal after another official withdrew. On match morning, severe back spasms make standing painful, and canceling would leave both teams unable to play, but six hours on the field could worsen his injury. Should Sanjay fulfill the officiating duty or withdraw to protect his recovery?

A: The maternity ward has recorded every newborn's footprint on a paper card kept by the family since the hospital opened. Director June proposes secure digital scans that are clearer and easier to retrieve, but nurses and parents value the inked card as a tangible rite. Should June replace the cards with digital records or preserve the footprint tradition?
B: A village orchestra has tuned to the same local pitch and opened concerts with its founder's march for generations. New conductor Pavel wants standard tuning and rotating contemporary openings so visiting musicians can join easily, while members fear losing their distinctive sound and ritual. Should Pavel modernize the orchestra's practice or continue its inherited musical customs?
C: A clinic removes patients from its waiting list after two missed appointments. Receptionist Alma learns that a homeless patient missed both because his shelter repeatedly changed locations; restoring him helps someone in hardship but bypasses others who complied and kept waiting. Should Alma make an exception for him or apply the same removal rule to every patient?

A: For decades, the courthouse has announced each morning's cases from a clerk's handwritten board in the entrance hall. Administrator Rosa wants electronic displays with live updates and translations, but veteran clerks and attorneys consider the board part of the building's civic character. Should Rosa install the displays or continue the courthouse's handwritten announcement tradition?
B: At a century-old baseball ground, attendants still change inning numbers by hand on a wooden scoreboard. The club can install a bright digital screen with instant statistics, but supporters value watching the attendant work and regard the board as part of every game. Should the club modernize the scoreboard or preserve the manual ritual?
C: A sanitation contractor offers inspector Greg free household trash collection if he approves diesel trucks that barely meet current limits. The perk would save him substantial fees, while the trucks would add noise and exhaust along routes serving thousands of residents. Should Greg accept the private benefit and approve the fleet or reject it to limit the community-wide cost?

A: Neighbors building the annual lantern festival have always shaped bamboo frames together in the school gym. Organizer Mei could order reusable metal frames that assemble faster and survive rain, but older volunteers say hand-building lanterns is where newcomers learn the community's stories. Should Mei switch to metal frames or retain the shared bamboo-making tradition?
B: The Bell family has harvested olives by spreading cloths and combing branches by hand for four generations. Daughter Lucia proposes a mechanical shaker that would finish before autumn storms and reduce labor, but her grandparents regard the communal hand harvest as the farm's defining custom. Should Lucia introduce the machine or continue harvesting in the traditional way?
C: Community garden chair Ezra discovers that his longtime friend submitted photographs from last year to claim completion of a current grant milestone. Reporting the truth could revoke funding and force his friend off the committee, while accepting the images misleads the foundation. Should Ezra correct the grant report or protect the friend who helped establish the garden?

A: A coding bootcamp gives every applicant exactly seventy-two hours to complete its entry project. Reviewer Nikhil learns that one applicant lost electricity throughout the deadline after her building burned, and she asks for three extra days, although previous late submissions were rejected. Should Nikhil grant her an extension or enforce the same deadline for everyone?
B: Volunteers receive one garden plot only if they attend three winter planning meetings. Coordinator Val knows a single father missed them while caring for a hospitalized child and needs the plot to grow food, but others arranged difficult schedules to qualify. Should Val waive the attendance rule for him or allocate plots strictly by the published requirement?
C: A hospital needs a medication-tracking update deployed by Friday before a regulatory inspection. Developer Ari can release the working version after limited testing, or spend another week checking rare dosage combinations and improving error messages, leaving staff on the old system during inspection. Should Ari deliver the update quickly or delay it to ensure dependable quality?

A: A dance academy bars students from the annual performance after more than four absences. Director Opal knows one talented dancer missed five rehearsals while moving between foster homes and sees how much the performance matters to her, while other students met the requirement. Should Opal let the dancer perform or apply the attendance rule equally?
B: A software conference refunds no tickets within seven days of opening. Organizer Dae receives a request from a freelancer whose premature baby requires unexpected hospital care; the ticket cost would help him travel to the child, although other late cancellations received nothing. Should Dae issue a compassionate refund or uphold the same policy for all attendees?
C: Sculptor Ines saved her commission payment to replace unsafe wiring in her studio before winter. A neighboring artist's dog is struck by a car and needs surgery tonight, but using the savings would leave Ines working around a serious electrical risk. Should Ines pay for the dog's treatment or keep the money for her own safety?

A: Professor Ahmed deducts ten points from every essay submitted after noon. One student delivers hers that evening after spending the morning translating for her mother at an asylum hearing, and the penalty would make her fail, while classmates accepted deductions for other emergencies. Should Ahmed excuse this late essay or apply the announced penalty equally?
B: A junior football academy releases any player who misses three mandatory practices. Coach Bruna's fastest winger reaches that limit because his family was evicted and he spent nights changing shelters, but several substitutes maintained perfect attendance. Should Bruna keep him on the squad because of his hardship or enforce the rule applied to everyone else?
C: Student adviser Milo wants to create a quiet woodworking club, although his parents and faculty colleagues consider it unsuitable for someone pursuing school leadership. They expect him to run the prestigious debate society and say senior staff will respect that choice. Should Milo start the club he personally wants or lead debate to gain their approval?

A: A farming cooperative fines members who deliver grain above the agreed moisture limit. Treasurer Ruth receives a damp load from an elderly farmer whose dryer failed and whose medical bills consumed his repair money; waiving the fine helps him survive but treats compliant farmers differently. Should Ruth excuse his penalty or apply the cooperative's rule without exception?
B: A scholarship requires every recipient to maintain eighty percent attendance. Administrator Joel sees that a refugee student fell just below the threshold while attending immigration appointments and will leave college without funding, yet other students lost awards under the same rule. Should Joel renew her scholarship as an exception or enforce the attendance standard equally?
C: A wholesaler wants three hundred peach crates packed by morning to catch the only train to market. Grower Helena can ship on time after quick visual sorting, or inspect every peach for bruising and miss the train, preserving quality but losing the week's buyers. Should Helena dispatch the crates quickly or delay them for careful inspection?

A: A laundromat charges the same replacement fee whenever customers lose a machine key. Owner Hamid meets an elderly customer who lost hers during an emergency evacuation and cannot afford both the fee and groceries, though everyone else has paid. Should Hamid replace her key without charge or follow the stated rule for every customer?
B: The housing office grants extensions only when repair applications arrive before a fixed cutoff. Clerk Sarah receives a late form from a tenant who was hospitalized and now faces a winter without heat, while several other late applicants were denied. Should Sarah accept his application because of the hardship or enforce the deadline consistently?
C: Bicycle shop owner Lian can stock an innovative folding bike from a new maker whose design might attract adventurous commuters but has little reliability history. A proven model sells steadily and includes dependable replacement parts, though it offers customers nothing new. Should Lian take a chance on the experimental bicycle or order the predictable established model?

A: Epidemiologist Marta has managed obsessive-compulsive disorder throughout her field study. Telling her research team could explain why certain travel arrangements matter and help colleagues discuss mental health honestly, but it would disclose a diagnosis she has concealed throughout her career. Should Marta share her condition with the team or keep her medical information private?
B: Actor Remy drew on his experience of bankruptcy to prepare for a new role. Describing that history during rehearsals could help the cast understand his choices and invite deeper collaboration, but his finances remain painfully personal and may become theater gossip. Should Remy tell the company about his bankruptcy or keep the source of his performance private?
C: A prestigious polar institute offers glaciologist Hana leadership of a five-year expedition program. The role would establish her internationally but require long absences from the laboratory friends who share meals, childcare, and daily life with her. Should Hana accept the position that advances her career or remain with the close research community she has built?

A: Team captain Zoe recently began treatment for an eating disorder. Explaining it to teammates could help them avoid harmful comments and understand why she sometimes trains separately, but the diagnosis is intimate and she fears it spreading through the league. Should Zoe speak openly with the team or keep her health information confidential?
B: Physician Elena is returning to work after caring for a partner with addiction. Sharing that experience at a staff meeting could help colleagues understand her interest in compassionate treatment and invite honest discussion, but it would expose her partner's private struggle as well as her own. Should Elena tell the department or keep the family experience private?
C: Boxer Marcus plans daily footwork drills for three months to correct a weakness before his next bout. Tonight his favorite restaurant is hosting a long tasting dinner, and the drills feel tedious after work, but skipping them weakens the consistency improvement requires. Should Marcus complete his training session or spend the evening enjoying the meal?

A: Nurse Adele has dyslexia and uses extra checks when recording medication. Telling her unit could help coworkers understand the process and build more candid safety practices, but she has never disclosed the diagnosis and worries it will redefine how they see her competence. Should Adele explain her dyslexia to colleagues or keep the information private?
B: Farmer Gideon is receiving counseling after panic attacks began during lambing season. Sharing this with neighboring farmers could explain why he now requests backup and encourage others to discuss similar problems, but his treatment feels deeply personal in their small community. Should Gideon speak openly about the panic attacks or keep his health history confidential?
C: A rehabilitation center requires patients who arrive intoxicated to miss that day's therapy group. Counselor Priya meets a homeless patient who relapsed after learning his sister died and may lose his housing placement without attendance, while others have been excluded under the rule. Should Priya admit him as an exception or enforce the same restriction?
